passage:
So, Nilesh, you asked me once what my worst online moment was. It's this. I'm Gurleen, and last spring I shared a post saying a girl called Meher from another college had cheated in an exam. It had a screenshot, and it was angry, and it felt like standing up for fairness. I didn't check it.

Two days later a friend sent me the college's statement: it was false. By then Meher was getting messages I wouldn't wish on anyone. My stomach dropped. My first thought was to say "well, I only shared it."

I didn't. I deleted it that night, posted a plain correction saying the claim was false and I was sorry I spread it, and messaged Meher directly to apologise. She read it and didn't reply. I understand.

qa.q: What did the post Gurleen shared claim about Meher?
qa.a: The post said Meher, a girl from another college, had cheated in an exam.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when the college's statement arrived, and what did Gurleen first want to say?
qa.a: Gurleen felt sick and ashamed, and first wanted to say "well, I only shared it", which was a way of protecting pride.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do that was right, and what else could help?
qa.a: Gurleen deleted the post, posted a plain correction and apologised to Meher directly; checking claims before sharing would help next time. 🤍

qa.q: How might Meher see Gurleen's apology?
qa.a: Meher read it and did not reply, which could mean she is still hurt by what happened, and Gurleen accepts that her silence is fair.

grounding: Gurleen realises a shared false claim hurt a person, feels ashamed, deletes it, posts a plain correction and apologises to her instead of defending it out of pride.

passage:
Monday. Before I even tried, I typed the whole assignment question into the AI. Even the email to the hostel warden. Dhruv, that's me, apparently. It felt faster, though it took me twenty minutes to figure out what I'd actually been asked to do.

Thursday. Manoj asked in class how our project's sorting step worked. I opened my mouth and there was nothing. My own thinking felt slow and rusty, like a bicycle left out in the rain. I said "I'll get back to you," which was true and embarrassing.

Next Tuesday. I set a timer for fifteen minutes and tried the problem on paper first. It was messy but mine. Then I asked the AI to check my steps and explain one I'd missed. This time I could explain it to Manoj at lunch.

qa.q: What did Manoj ask about in class on Thursday?
qa.a: Manoj asked how the project's sorting step worked.

qa.q: How did Dhruv feel when the answer would not come on Thursday?
qa.a: Dhruv felt slow and rusty, like a bicycle left out in the rain, and embarrassed to say "I'll get back to you".

qa.q: What changed on Tuesday, and why is it a wiser way to use AI?
qa.a: Dhruv tried the problem on paper for fifteen minutes first, then asked the AI to check and explain a missed step, so the skill stayed Dhruv's own.

qa.q: How might Manoj have seen Dhruv's silence on Thursday and the explanation later?
qa.a: Manoj may have been surprised by the silence, but the clear explanation at lunch showed Dhruv now understood the step, not just the answer.

grounding: Dhruv asks the AI before trying and feels slower, then over days tries first, uses AI to check and can explain the work.

passage:
Tarun, remember the essay I nearly failed over? Here's the real story. I'm Nilesh, and I used to treat the AI like the smartest person in the room. It always answered in one calm, confident paragraph, and I just accepted it.

For my history essay I asked for a quote about the famine, and it gave me one, with a book title and a page number. I put it straight in. Sounded perfect.

The librarian said, "I can't find that book." I asked the AI for a source and it gave me a slightly different title. That's when my stomach sank: neither existed.

Now for facts I ask for sources and check them myself. For anything about health, law or money, I go to a qualified person, not just a fluent answer.

qa.q: What did the AI give Nilesh for the history essay?
qa.a: It gave a quote about the famine with a book title and a page number.

qa.q: What did Nilesh feel when the librarian could not find the book?
qa.a: Nilesh's stomach sank, realising that the confident answer had nothing behind it and that neither book existed.

qa.q: What would you advise someone who gets a confident AI answer?
qa.a: Trust but verify: ask for sources, check them, and for health, law or money go to a qualified person instead of relying on fluent text. 🙂

qa.q: How might the librarian have seen Nilesh's quote?
qa.a: The librarian probably saw a quote that could not be traced and had to say so plainly, which helped Nilesh see the gap before the essay was marked.

grounding: Nilesh accepted the AI's confident answers until a false source showed fluent text is not truth, and now verifies claims.

passage:
Vaibhav: You're up at midnight again. Who are you texting?
Yamini: My companion app. It's easy. It never judges me.
Vaibhav: Nothing judges you when it just agrees.
Yamini: That's not fair. It listens. Today I told it about my presentation and it made me feel better.
Vaibhav: Good. I mean that. But when did we last have chai together?
Yamini: ...I skipped Priya's birthday last week, didn't I.
Vaibhav: You did. She asked about you.
Yamini: People are harder. They get tired, they say the wrong thing.
Vaibhav: They also come to your door when you're sick. Keep the app for the hard nights. Come for chai on Saturday too.
Yamini: Okay. Saturday. I'll text Priya first.

qa.q: Whose birthday did Yamini skip last week?
qa.a: Yamini skipped Priya's birthday last week.

qa.q: Why does Yamini find the companion app easier than people?
qa.a: The app never judges Yamini and always listens, while people get tired and can say the wrong thing.

qa.q: What would you advise Yamini to do?
qa.a: Enjoy the comfort of the app, but keep growing human bonds by going for chai on Saturday and texting Priya, because real friends can show up in ways software cannot.

qa.q: How might Priya feel about Yamini missing the birthday?
qa.a: Priya asked about Yamini, so she likely felt missed and a little hurt, and a message from Yamini could repair it. 🙂

grounding: An AI companion feels easier than people for Yamini because it never judges, while a friend encourages keeping human bonds growing.

passage:
Prof. Divyansh: Binita, please sit. This paragraph reads very differently from your earlier work. Did you use an AI tool?
Binita: (heart pounding) ...Yes. Partly.
Prof. Divyansh: Which part?
Binita: The summary section, and I asked it to polish my sentences. The analysis is mine. I have my handwritten notes and the first draft here.
Prof. Divyansh: Thank you for saying so directly. Show me the notes.
Binita: (sliding over the pages) I didn't read the course rules properly. I thought polishing was fine.
Prof. Divyansh: The rule asks you to declare any use. Let's read it together, then we can decide what to do with this submission.
Binita: Okay. I should have asked first.

qa.q: Which parts did Binita say came from the AI tool?
qa.a: Binita said the summary section and the sentence polishing came from the tool, while the analysis was Binita's own.

qa.q: How did Binita feel when the professor asked about the AI tool, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Exposed and nervous: Binita's heart was pounding before the answer, which came after a pause.

qa.q: What did Binita do that kept a small matter small?
qa.a: Binita told the truth, showed handwritten notes and the first draft, and agreed to learn the rules, instead of lying.

qa.q: How might Prof. Divyansh see Binita's honesty?
qa.a: Prof. Divyansh thanked Binita for saying it directly, so honesty and visible process make it easier to treat this as a rule to learn than as cheating.

grounding: A professor suspects an AI-written assignment when it was partly so, and Binita admits it honestly, shows process and learns the rules.

passage:
The computer lab closed at nine, Tarun's data pack had almost run out, and the problem set was due at midnight. Tarun worked through question after question by hand, erasing and trying again, hunched over one desk in a noisy corridor.

Across the room, Anand finished the whole set in ten minutes with an AI tool, closed the laptop and left for tea. Next week the marks came back: Anand scored higher. Tarun felt foolish, as if hours of effort had bought nothing.

A month later, at a mock interview, the panel asked Anand to explain one solution on the whiteboard. Anand's marker stayed still.

Tarun, on the other hand, had used the AI as a tutor that night, asking it to explain the one step that didn't click, and could walk through every line.

qa.q: What time did the computer lab close?
qa.a: The computer lab closed at nine.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel when the marks came back, and why?
qa.a: Tarun felt foolish, as if hours of effort had bought nothing, because Anand scored higher after finishing in ten minutes.

qa.q: What did Tarun do with the AI that helped later?
qa.a: Tarun used it as a tutor to explain the one step that didn't click, so Tarun could walk through every line, while Anand copied without understanding.

qa.q: How might Anand feel at the mock interview?
qa.a: Anand probably felt exposed and stuck, with the marker staying still, because the shortcut left no understanding to explain.

grounding: Tarun envies Anand's quick, high-scoring AI work and feels foolish, but shortcuts show at the interview while using AI as a tutor builds real skill.

passage:
Dear Salma,

I've been meaning to write since our chat last week. You asked how training is going, and I said "fine". It isn't. I'm training to become a translator, and every week there's a new video of an AI translating a page in seconds. Last night I lay awake doing the maths on whether I'll have a job in five years. My chest gets tight just typing that.

I know the worry makes sense. But I also know freezing won't help. So I've started using the tools for first drafts and correcting them, which is teaching me where they get tone and idiom wrong. That feels like a skill.

Can we talk this weekend about which human parts of the work I should get better at?

Kiran

qa.q: What is Kiran training to become?
qa.a: Kiran is training to become a translator.

qa.q: How does Kiran feel about the future, and what shows it?
qa.a: Kiran is anxious: lying awake doing the maths on a job in five years and feeling the chest get tight.

qa.q: What is Kiran doing that is wiser than freezing or denial?
qa.a: Kiran uses the tools for first drafts and corrects them, learning where they miss tone and idiom, and wants to build the human parts of the work.

qa.q: How might Salma react to Kiran's letter?
qa.a: Salma may be touched that Kiran finally admitted it isn't fine, and the question about human skills invites a practical talk instead of reassurance alone.

grounding: Kiran worries AI will take the job Kiran is training for and responds by learning the tools and building judgement rather than freezing.

Dear Keerthana,

Three months into the job and I wanted to tell you something. My manager wants twenty report summaries a day, made with the AI tool, and I've never once been asked whether I understand them. Speed is all that gets praised.

Last Thursday I found a wrong figure in a summary that had already gone to a client. It was the tool's mistake, but I sent it without checking. My hands went cold. My first thought was to say "the software did it."

Instead I told my manager the same day, showed the correct figure and offered to check the other summaries from that week. The manager just said "okay, fix it". Not warm, but fine.

From now on I check every number myself.

Ayesha

qa.q: How many report summaries a day does the manager want?
qa.a: The manager wants twenty report summaries a day.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel on finding the wrong figure, and what was the first thought?
qa.a: Ayesha felt panicked: Ayesha's hands went cold, and the first thought was to hide behind the tool by saying "the software did it".

qa.q: What did Ayesha do that was right, and what will change?
qa.a: Ayesha told the manager the same day, showed the correct figure and offered to recheck the week's summaries; from now on Ayesha will check every number personally. 🙂

qa.q: How does the manager seem to see the mistake?
qa.a: The manager said "okay, fix it", not warmly, which suggests the concern is correcting the work quickly, not asking whether Ayesha understands it.

grounding: An employer expects AI-level speed and never asks about understanding, so Ayesha checks accuracy personally and speaks up about the error.

passage:
Ivan stood at the window of his Warsaw student flat, holding a vape he'd told himself was "just for exam weeks". That had been true once. Now it was the first thing he reached for after lectures, and the thing he reached for when the flat felt too quiet. "I can stop anytime," he'd said to himself again this morning.

That evening Beatriz, a friend from his course, noticed his hands shaking slightly at the café. "You've missed two labs," she said gently.

Ivan opened his notes app and counted honestly: missed labs, money spent, the mornings he felt flat. He read the list out loud, slowly.

"I think I need help," he said. Beatriz nodded. "The university health service does this. I'll come with you if you want."

Ivan booked it that night.

qa.q: What was Ivan holding at the window?
qa.a: Ivan was holding a vape he'd told himself was just for exam weeks.

qa.q: What is Ivan worried about or hiding from himself, and what shifts once the cost is counted?
qa.a: He kept saying he could stop anytime, but counting the missed labs, money and flat mornings honestly made him say he needed help.

qa.q: What would you advise Ivan to do next?
qa.a: Keep the appointment with the university health service, keep telling Beatriz, and avoid hiding it or calling it stress relief. 🤍

qa.q: How might Beatriz see Ivan's situation?
qa.a: Beatriz saw shaking hands and two missed labs and spoke gently instead of accusing, showing concern for a friend and offering to go along.

grounding: Ivan's occasional habit has become his way of coping and he says he can stop anytime, until he counts the cost, tells a friend and seeks help.

passage:
Sunday, 2 a.m.

Friday I promised myself never again. I wrote it on a sticky note and stuck it to the mirror. Last night I drank again anyway. Woke up hating myself. I said things in my head I'd never say to a friend: weak, pathetic, useless.

And then I noticed something: every time I feel like that, the next thing I want is another drink, just to switch off the voice. The hating is part of the loop.

Chaitanya texted this morning, "Call me anytime. No lecture." I hadn't told Chaitanya anything, but somehow it landed.

So tonight I'm writing it as facts: Friday, alone, after the fight with my sister. That's a trigger. Tomorrow I'll call Chaitanya and ask about the campus counsellor.

Pradeep

qa.q: What did Pradeep write on the sticky note?
qa.a: Pradeep wrote a promise of never again on a sticky note and stuck it to the mirror.

qa.q: What does Pradeep notice about the hating feeling, and why does it matter?
qa.a: The self-hate makes Pradeep want another drink to switch off the voice, so the shame is part of the loop instead of a cure.

qa.q: What steps is Pradeep planning, and how do they treat the relapse?
qa.a: Pradeep treats it as data, naming the trigger of Friday alone after the fight with the sister, then plans to call Chaitanya and ask about the campus counsellor.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see Pradeep's struggle?
qa.a: Chaitanya seems to sense something is wrong and offers a call with no lecture, so support without judgement is what Chaitanya wants to give. 🤍

grounding: After each binge Pradeep promises never again and relapses with self-hatred, then sees shame fuels the cycle, treats relapse as data and seeks support.
